titolo: Switzerland Should Be Poor. Here's Why It Isn't

numero.sotto: ONE PRODUCT, SOLD IN NEW PACKAGES

descrizione:
Two hundred years ago, Swiss villagers ate grass and tree bark. Today Switzerland is one of the richest countries on Earth, with no sea, no oil, no gold mines and mountains everywhere. How did that happen? We follow 500 years of one strange product: safety, sold in new packages, from mercenaries to neutrality, vaults and medicine.

We walk through the lucky accidents that built the Swiss fortune, the bills that came due for banking secrecy, and the skill that keeps the country rich anyway: recovery. Every border has a price, and here is Switzerland's.

scene.testo: Shelters for everyone. A bank that fell in one weekend. Soldiers for rent. Gold nobody should have kept. How does a poor mountain rock get this rich?
In 1817, in the eastern Swiss mountains, people ate grass and tree bark. That year, twice the usual number of Swiss died.
The summer before, snow had fallen down to the valley floors. A volcano called Tambora, on the other side of the planet, had stolen Europe's summer.
The harvest failed. Some villages grew so poor that they later paid their own neighbors to leave for America.
Today, that same country is the fourth richest on Earth per person. And that makes no sense.
Switzerland has no sea, no oil, no gas, no gold mines. About sixty percent of it is mountain, land you can barely farm.
Four languages. No colonies. Surrounded for centuries by empires far bigger than itself. So how does this landlocked rock end up so rich?
We need three answers. What did Switzerland sell when it had nothing? Why did the richest people trust it? And why is the model cracking?
The answer is strange. For 500 years, Switzerland has sold the world the same product, only in different packages.
Start with the map. Mountains are a wall. They protect you, but they also trap you.
No big river to the sea. No wide plains for huge farms. Every valley was its own little world.
So for most of its history, Switzerland was poor. Too many people, too little land. And poor mountain countries export what they have too much of: young men.
Swiss pikemen became the most feared soldiers in Europe. Kings, dukes and popes rented them by the thousand.
This was no side business. Around 1500, about one in eight Swiss was serving as a soldier for someone else.
Over the centuries, about one and a half million Swiss men marched off to foreign wars. Up to forty percent never came home.
In 1506, a pope hired a unit of them as bodyguards. That unit still guards the Vatican today.
Sometimes Swiss mercenaries even faced each other in one battle, paid by two different kings to kill one another.
The money came home in the pockets of survivors. By the 1800s, less than fifteen percent of Swiss coins were actually Swiss.
So Switzerland's first export wasn't cheese or watches. It was safety, paid for in blood.
Then, in 1515, at Marignano in northern Italy, the Swiss lost badly to the French.
And instead of revenge, they did something almost no power did. They stopped expanding and chose to stay out of other people's wars.
For three centuries, neutrality was only a habit. Then Napoleon's armies swept through anyway, proving a habit is not a shield.

eventi.descrizione: French emperor, bicorne hat, grey coat

eventi.testo: A habit is not a shield

scene.testo: But when Napoleon fell, Europe's great powers redrew the map. On November 20, 1815, they signed a guarantee that Switzerland would stay neutral forever.
Think about that. On a continent that went to war every generation, one country held a legal promise to stay out.
If you are rich and your country might burn, where do you keep your money? Switzerland now sold the promise that nothing would happen there.
But a promise feeds no one. As late as 1855, one Swiss village paid for 305 of its people to leave for America. More than one in ten.
Over the century, more than half a million Swiss left. Neutral? Yes. Rich? Not even close.
To get rich, Switzerland needed a few lucky accidents. The first happened in Geneva. In 1541, the reformer John Calvin banned jewelry as sinful.

eventi.descrizione: 16th-century Protestant reformer, black robe, stern face

scene.testo: Geneva's goldsmiths suddenly had no market. So they turned their tiny tools to something Calvin could not object to: clocks.
French Protestant refugees brought even more skill. By 1601, Geneva had the world's first watchmakers guild. A religious ban had created an industry built on precision.
Keep those watchmakers in mind. Four hundred years later, they almost disappear.
Accident number two: chaos. Before 1850, Switzerland had no single money. About eight thousand different coins and banknotes circulated.
Then the new federal state created one currency, the franc. It sounds boring, but it became one of the most trusted currencies on Earth.
It would be so trusted that one day it would become a problem. Hold that thought.
Accident number three: the wall became a road. In 1882, the Swiss opened a 15 kilometer railway tunnel under the Gotthard Pass, the longest in the world.
It cost at least 177 workers their lives. When workers went on strike, the army opened fire and killed four.
But once open, the mountain wall was suddenly a toll road between northern and southern Europe.

eventi.testo: The wall became a trade route

scene.testo: Accident number four came in Basel, on the Rhine. In 1859, a silk dyer began making the new artificial dyes just discovered in England.
Others followed. Dye factories became chemical companies, and chemical companies grew into some of the biggest pharmaceutical firms in the world.
Accident number five happened in the lakeside town of Vevey. In 1875, Daniel Peter finally mixed cocoa with condensed milk: milk chocolate.
His neighbor, by the way, was a man named Henri Nestlé.
Watches, a trusted franc, a tunnel, medicine, chocolate. Notice the pattern. None needs oil, a port or an empire.
They are small, expensive things you buy because you trust they will not fail. If you like seeing how maps decide who gets rich, subscribe.
But none of that explains the real Swiss fortune. For that, we have to go underground, into the vaults.
In 1932, France launched a campaign against its own tax evaders. Rich French families panicked, and Switzerland answered.
In 1934, a new banking law made revealing a client's information a federal crime. A banker who talked could go to prison.
Even your own government could ask. Even your tax office could ask. The answer was silence.
In June 1940, days after France fell, Germany drew up a plan to invade Switzerland. Up to half a million men.
After conquest, the country would be carved up by language. German part to Germany, Italian to Italy, French to France.
The Swiss answer was to pull the army back into the mountains, into a fortress carved inside the Alps, ready to fight for years.
The invasion never came, but that fortress mindset never left. In 1963, a law promised every resident a place in a nuclear shelter.
Today there are around 370,000 shelters. That is enough to fit the whole population, so a country that sells safety also buys it for everyone.
During the war, Switzerland kept doing business with everyone, including Nazi Germany. A later commission found its national bank took in about 1.6 billion francs in German gold.
About three quarters of that gold had been looted from other countries. And the bank's leaders knew early on where it came from.
The same mountains that sheltered refugees' savings also stored stolen gold. The vaults did not ask questions. That was the product.
But the thing that made Switzerland rich was about to become its biggest problem. Because secrets have a price, and the bill was coming.
Bill number one arrived in 1995. Families of Holocaust victims asked: where is the money our relatives left in your banks?
Swiss secrecy made even that hard to answer. It became the country's biggest diplomatic crisis since the war.
In 1998, its two giant banks agreed to pay one and a quarter billion dollars, eventually reaching more than 450,000 claimants.
Bill number two came in 2009. America caught UBS running secret accounts for about 20,000 US clients, around 17,000 of them hiding money from the tax office.
UBS paid 780 million dollars. And then it did the unthinkable: it handed over client names.
Bill number three, 2018. Switzerland began automatically sending account data to tax authorities across Europe and beyond. About two million accounts in the first round.
The secret was over. And bill number four came in March 2023, when Credit Suisse, one of the oldest names in Swiss banking, began to fall.
In just three months, clients pulled out 61 billion francs. Then, over one weekend, the government pushed UBS to buy it for 3 billion.
It came with up to 200 billion francs in state guarantees. The country that sold trust watched one of its biggest banks collapse in two days.

eventi.testo: The trust seller lost its bank

scene.testo: And in 2025, for the first time, Hong Kong caught up with Switzerland as the world's biggest hub for money from abroad.
So the secret is gone. One giant bank is gone. The crown is slipping. Why is Switzerland still this rich?
Because banking was never the whole story. Remember Basel? That one city is home to two of the ten biggest pharmaceutical companies on Earth.
Medicines alone make up more than a third of everything Switzerland exports. Safety still sells, it just comes in a pill bottle now.

eventi.testo: Medicine is a third of exports

scene.testo: Remember the watchmakers? In 1969, a Japanese company released the first quartz watch, cheaper and more accurate than any Swiss one.
Within 15 years, Swiss watchmaking jobs fell from 90,000 to about 30,000. The industry Calvin accidentally created was dying.

eventi.testo: Two thirds of the jobs vanished

scene.testo: Then, in 1983, it came back with a cheap, colorful, plastic watch: the Swatch. That is the real Swiss skill. Not the secret. The recovery.
It is built into the system. About two thirds of Swiss teenagers choose an apprenticeship, learning a trade inside a real company while they study.
Citizens also vote directly on laws several times a year, which makes wild political swings rare.
And the franc became so trusted that the central bank had to hold it down by force. In January 2015, it let go.
The franc jumped about twenty percent within minutes. Most countries fear their money collapsing. Switzerland's problem is that the whole world wants its.
When Switzerland had nothing, it sold safety. The rich trusted it because it was the one place in Europe where nothing happened.
The model cracks because the world stopped accepting silence. Yet safety still sells. Pikes, neutrality, vaults, medicine: 500 years, one product, from grass to riches.
